passages.t: The priest goes outside the camp
passages.happening:
“This is the law for the one afflicted with a skin disease on the day of his cleansing” (verse 2). “The priest is to go outside the camp to examine him” (verse 3).

If the person has healed, the priest calls for two live clean birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn and hyssop. One bird is killed over fresh water in a clay pot. The living bird is dipped, with the wood, yarn and hyssop, in the blood and water. The priest sprinkles the person seven times. “Then he shall pronounce him clean and release the live bird into the open field” (verse 7).

The person washes his clothes, shaves off all his hair and bathes. “Afterward, he may enter the camp, but he must remain outside his tent for seven days” (verse 8). On the seventh day he shaves and washes again (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 13 sent a person out of the camp. Chapter 14 is the road home. It says something about this book that it spends a whole chapter, and one of its fullest ceremonies, on bringing back someone who had been shut out. The God who lives among Israel is not content to keep the unclean away. He provides the way for them to return.

The first step is taken by the priest. The sick person could not come in, so the priest goes out to him.

The priest does not heal. The person has already recovered. The rite marks and announces what has happened, and brings him back by stages.

The things used are linked with life and cleansing elsewhere in the law. ‘Fresh water’ is, word for word, living water: water that runs. Hyssop is a small bushy plant used for sprinkling, as on the night of the first Passover. One bird dies. The other, dipped in its blood, flies free over the open field, a living sign that the uncleanness has gone. The same shape, one creature killed and one sent away, comes again with the two goats of the Day of Atonement in chapter 16.

Shaving all the hair marks a fresh start, a little like being born again into the community.

The return comes in three steps over the chapter, each closer than the last: first into the camp, then into his own tent, then to the sanctuary.
passages.later:
On the night of the first Passover, Israel was told, “Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin, and brush the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe” (Exodus 12:22).

David used the picture when he prayed after his sin: “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow” (Psalm 51:7).

When Jesus healed a man with a skin disease, he sent him to do what this chapter says: “go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing” (Mark 1:44). A priest would have found himself confirming a healing that had already taken place.
passages.asks: The priest went out to the person who could not come in. Ask who cannot come to where you are, and whether you could go to them. And ask whether your church has a way of bringing people back, or only ways of letting them go.

passages.t: The eighth day: blood and oil
passages.happening:
“On the eighth day he is to bring two unblemished male lambs, an unblemished ewe lamb a year old”, a grain offering and a small measure of oil (verse 10). The priest presents him, with his offerings, before the LORD at the entrance to the tent (verse 11).

One lamb is offered as a guilt offering. The priest takes some of its blood and puts it “on the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot” (verse 14). He sprinkles some of the oil seven times before the LORD, and puts oil on the same three places, over the blood. The rest of the oil he puts on the person's head (verses 15-18).

Then come the sin offering and the burnt offering with the grain offering, “to make atonement for him, and he will be clean” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
An attentive reader has seen this before. Blood on the right ear, the right thumb and the right big toe is what Moses did to Aaron and his sons when he made them priests (8:23-24).

The person who had lived outside the camp, dressed like a mourner and calling out a warning, is brought back with a rite that echoes the ordination of the priests. He is not let in by a side door. He is received with honor, and set apart for God from head to foot. Then oil is poured on his head.

Why a guilt offering, when no wrong is named? Readers differ. Some think that during the long time away, offerings owed to God had gone unpaid, and this makes them good. Others see it simply as part of setting the restored person apart.

The word ‘atonement’ comes several times in this passage, though no sin is mentioned. In Leviticus the word is wider than the forgiveness of wrongs. It covers the removal of whatever keeps a person from God's presence, uncleanness included.

The key word of the chapter is ‘clean’. The Hebrew verb comes nineteen times, more than in chapter 13. The weight has moved from finding the disease to bringing the person home.
passages.later:
The ordination of the priests used the same marks: Moses put blood “on Aaron’s right earlobe, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot” (Leviticus 8:23).

The letter to the Hebrews compares such rites with what Christ has done: “how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences” (Hebrews 9:14). The comparison is the New Testament's own, and it honors what it compares. As the notes on Hebrews 8 say, a shadow is real.
passages.asks: The outcast was welcomed home with a rite like a priest's. Ask how your church receives a person coming back after a long time away: with suspicion, or with honor. And ask who has come back into your own life whom you have never properly welcomed.

passages.happening:
“If, however, the person is poor and cannot afford these offerings”, he brings one male lamb as a guilt offering, a smaller grain offering, the oil, “and two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he can afford” (verses 21-22).

The priest does for him everything he did in the fuller rite: the blood on ear, thumb and toe, the oil sprinkled and put on the same places, the oil on his head (verses 23-29). The birds are offered as the sin offering and the burnt offering (verses 30-31).

“This is the law for someone who has a skin disease and cannot afford the cost of his cleansing” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Three lambs were a heavy cost. And a person who had lived outside the camp for months or years, away from field and work, may well have had little left.

So the law comes down to meet him. One lamb in place of three. Birds in place of the others. A third of the flour.

What is not reduced is the rite. Every act is told again in full for the poor person: the blood, the oil, the three marks, the oil on the head. The text could have said that the priest does as before. It writes it all out. The poor are given the whole ceremony, and the words ‘whichever he can afford’ come twice.

This is the third time in the book that the cost is lowered for those with little (5:7; 12:8). No one was to be kept outside because of what the way back cost.
passages.later:
Jesus named the healing of people with this disease among the signs of his work, in the same breath as good news for the poor: “the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor” (Matthew 11:5).

When ten were healed and only one came back to give thanks, Jesus asked, “Were not all ten cleansed?” and then, “Where then are the other nine?” (Luke 17:17).
passages.asks: The law would not let the cost of coming home keep anyone out. Ask what it costs, in money, clothes, time or confidence, to belong where you worship. And ask who is staying away because they think they cannot afford to come back.

passages.happening:
The LORD speaks of the time “When you enter the land of Canaan, which I am giving you as your possession” (verse 34). If mildew appears in a house, the owner tells the priest, ‘Something like mildew has appeared in my house’ (verse 35).

The priest orders the house emptied before he goes in, “so that nothing in the house will become unclean” (verse 36). If the marks look deeper than the surface, he closes the house for seven days (verse 38). If they have spread, the bad stones are pulled out, the walls scraped and replastered (verses 40-42). If the mildew comes back and spreads, the house is pulled down (verses 44-45).

If it does not come back, the priest pronounces the house clean, and cleanses it with the rite of the two birds. “In this way he will make atonement for the house, and it will be clean” (verse 53).
passages.hearers:
This law looks ahead. In the wilderness Israel lived in tents. In the land they would live in houses of stone or mudbrick with plastered walls and wooden beams, where damp and mold were real troubles.

The method is the one already used for skin and cloth: report, look, wait seven days, look again. And the same care not to destroy in haste. Bad stones are replaced first. Only a house that cannot be saved is pulled down.

One detail is kind. The priest has the house emptied before he looks at it. Until he has pronounced on it, nothing in it counts as unclean. The family's belongings are spared.

A house can be given ‘atonement’. A wall has not sinned. This shows once more how wide the word is in this book.
passages.later:
Jesus used the picture of a house and its foundations for a whole life: “everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock” (Matthew 7:24).

The psalms say where the safety of any house finally rests: “Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1).
passages.hard:
Verse 34 has God say, ‘I put a contamination of mildew into a house’. Does God send such things as punishment?

Some interpreters take this as the Old Testament's usual way of speaking about God's rule over everything that happens. On this reading it carries no thought of punishment. Nothing in the passage says the owner has done wrong. Others link it with places where the same Hebrew word describes a blow that comes as judgment, and later Jewish interpretation sometimes tied such outbreaks to sins like slander. The text itself makes no such link, and a reader should be slow to supply one.

That caution matters beyond mildew. No one should read a damp wall, an illness or a loss as a message about someone's hidden sin. No one should be told that their illness or disability is a punishment.
passages.asks: The priest emptied the house first, so that a family's goods were not lost with the wall. Ask how you could put something right in your home, church or work in a way that spares people as much loss as possible. And ask what small sign of rot you have been ignoring that would be easier to deal with now than later.
